title: Jeremiah 31:1–14
context: The consolation continues. The LORD promises to be the God of all the families of Israel (31:1) and recalls the people who survived the sword and found favor in the wilderness (31:2), an image many readers connect with the exodus and others with the survivors of the exile. In 31:3 Jeremiah recounts the LORD appearing to him of old with the words “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.” Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s love for his people is everlasting and is the source of his drawing; the broader question of how God draws people is covered at John 6:44 and is not restated here. In 31:4–6 the LORD promises to rebuild the virgin of Israel, with tambourines, dances, and vineyards on the mountains of Samaria, and watchmen in Ephraim calling the people up to Zion, so the northern tribes and Jerusalem worship together again. In 31:7–9 the LORD commands songs for Jacob and promises to gather the remnant from the north country, including the blind, the lame, and women with child, leading them with weeping and petitions, for he is a father to Israel and Ephraim is his firstborn (compare Exodus 4:22). In 31:10–14 the nations hear that the one who scattered Israel will gather him like a shepherd, that the LORD has ransomed Jacob, and that Zion will rejoice in grain, wine, oil, and flocks, with mourning turned to joy.

verses.text: “At that time,” says the LORD, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be my people.”
verses.arminianNotes: “At that time … I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be my people.” Arminian readers see the covenant offered to every family of Israel, north and south, and they hear in “all” the breadth of God’s saving intention toward his people, which the families are called to receive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same promise as God’s pledge to make the covenant relationship real in all the families he gathers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing the covenant formula of 30:22, and both see “At that time” linking it with the restoration and the latter days just announced (30:24).

verses.text: The LORD says, “The people who survive the sword found favor in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The people who survive the sword found favor in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.” Arminian readers hear grace shown to survivors, recalling the wilderness after the exodus, and they see God’s past favor as the ground for trusting his future care. Some readers apply the image instead to the exiles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see favor in the wilderness as unearned grace, given when Israel had nothing, and they read God’s going “to cause him to rest” as his initiative. Shared ground: both traditions hear an echo of the exodus and wilderness journey, and both see the LORD’s past mercy as a pledge of renewed mercy after exile, whichever survivors are first in view.

verses.text: The LORD appeared of old to me, saying, “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.” Arminian readers rejoice in God’s steadfast covenant love for Israel and hear the drawing as gracious, persistent kindness that woos his people back. They do not read the verse as settling the scope of individual election.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers rejoice in the same everlasting love and often connect “Therefore I have drawn you” with God’s love as the cause of his drawing. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a declaration of God’s faithful love for his people that grounds their restoration; the broader question of how God draws is covered at John 6:44 and is not restated here.

verses.text: I will build you again, and you will be built, O virgin of Israel. You will again be adorned with your tambourines, and will go out in the dances of those who make merry.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will build you again, and you will be built, O virgin of Israel … adorned with your tambourines.” Arminian readers note that the people once condemned for unfaithfulness are now called “virgin,” a sign of restored honor, and they see joy and dancing as the free response of a people renewed by grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the double statement, “I will build … you will be built,” as God’s certain work, and they hear the title “virgin” as grace that covers past shame. Shared ground: both traditions read the tambourines and dances as celebration recalling Israel’s songs after deliverance (compare Exodus 15:20), and both see restored joy as a gift of the LORD.

verses.text: Again you will plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. The planters will plant, and will enjoy its fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: “Again you will plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. The planters will plant, and will enjoy its fruit.” Arminian readers see the northern territory restored and normal life resumed, with planters enjoying their own labor, a reversal of the curse of losing one’s harvest to others (compare Deuteronomy 28:30).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same picture as covenant blessing restored by God’s faithfulness, and they note that Samaria, once a symbol of apostasy, becomes fruitful again. Shared ground: both traditions read the vineyards as peace and settled life, and both see the promise including the northern tribes in the restoration.

verses.text: For there will be a day that the watchmen on the hills of Ephraim cry, ‘Arise! Let’s go up to Zion to the LORD our God.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD foresees a day when “the watchmen on the hills of Ephraim cry, ‘Arise! Let’s go up to Zion to the LORD our God.’” Arminian readers see a striking reversal: Ephraim, once divided from Jerusalem’s worship, now calls the people to go up to Zion, and they see a renewed people choosing to worship together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reunion as God healing the old division between north and south and drawing both to one place of worship. Shared ground: both traditions read the watchmen’s call as the end of the schism that began after Solomon (compare 1 Kings 12:26–33), and both see united worship as the goal of restoration.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “Sing with gladness for Jacob, and shout for the chief of the nations. Publish, praise, and say, ‘LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel!’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands, “Sing with gladness for Jacob … ‘LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel!’” Arminian readers hear joy and prayer joined: the people praise God for what he promises while still asking him to save, which shows salvation as both gift and the object of faithful prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God himself commands the prayer for the remnant’s salvation, which he has already promised to answer, so prayer is the means he appoints. Shared ground: both traditions read the remnant as the survivors whom God preserves, and the site’s discussions at Joshua 10:14 on prayer and Romans 11:5 on the remnant cover the deeper questions.

verses.text: Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the uttermost parts of the earth, along with the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her who travails with child together. They will return as a great company.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring them from the north country … along with the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her who travails with child together.” Arminian readers see tender inclusion: the weakest are not left behind, and God’s gathering reaches those who could never make the journey by their own strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same inclusion as a sign that the gathering depends wholly on God, since the company is marked by weakness, not strength. Shared ground: both traditions read the “great company” as the LORD’s gracious gathering of the scattered (compare 3:18; 23:8), and both see the vulnerable as especially cared for.

verses.text: They will come with weeping. I will lead them with petitions. I will cause them to walk by rivers of waters, in a straight way in which they won’t stumble; for I am a father to Israel. Ephraim is my firstborn.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will come with weeping. I will lead them with petitions … for I am a father to Israel. Ephraim is my firstborn.” Arminian readers see repentant tears and prayer accompanying the return, and they see God’s fatherly care guiding a responsive people on a straight way where they will not stumble.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD leading his children as a father, with Ephraim called “my firstborn” as an act of covenant grace (compare Exodus 4:22), and they hear the weeping and petitions as fruits of grace. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as tender fatherly love, and both see repentance and divine leading belonging together.

verses.text: “Hear the LORD’s word, you nations, and declare it in the distant islands. Say, ‘He who scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him, as a shepherd does his flock.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the nations, “He who scattered Israel will gather him, and keep him, as a shepherd does his flock.” Arminian readers note that the nations are invited to hear and declare God’s faithfulness, and they see the shepherd image as patient care that keeps the flock in his protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the one who scattered is the one who gathers, so judgment and restoration both lie in the LORD’s hand, and they hear “keep him” as God’s preserving care. Shared ground: both traditions read the shepherd image as covenant care (compare 23:3; Ezekiel 34:11–16), and both see the gathering as a witness to the nations.

verses.text: For the LORD has ransomed Jacob, and redeemed him from the hand of him who was stronger than he.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the LORD has ransomed Jacob, and redeemed him from the hand of him who was stronger than he.” Arminian readers see redemption as God’s mighty act on behalf of a helpless people, and they note that Christian readers in their tradition commonly hear an anticipation of the fuller redemption accomplished in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that Jacob was overpowered by a stronger hand and could not free himself, so redemption is entirely the LORD’s work; many in this tradition also hear it as pointing to redemption in Christ. Shared ground: both traditions read “ransomed” and “redeemed” as exodus language applied to the return from exile, and both see deliverance as grace.

verses.text: They will come and sing in the height of Zion, and will flow to the goodness of the LORD, to the grain, to the new wine, to the oil, and to the young of the flock and of the herd. Their soul will be as a watered garden. They will not sorrow any more at all.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will come and sing in the height of Zion … Their soul will be as a watered garden. They will not sorrow any more at all.” Arminian readers see joyful worship and abundant provision as the experience of a people who return to God and find him good, satisfying body and soul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same abundance as the LORD’s gift, with the people flowing to his goodness rather than earning it, and many hear an anticipation of final joy. Shared ground: both traditions read grain, wine, oil, and flocks as covenant blessing, and both hear the “watered garden” as a picture of a life renewed by God (compare Isaiah 58:11).

verses.text: Then the virgin will rejoice in the dance, the young men and the old together; for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the virgin will rejoice in the dance … for I will turn their mourning into joy.” Arminian readers see restored joy across generations, young and old together, and they hear God’s comfort as a gracious answer to the sorrow that repentance and loss had brought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who turns mourning into joy and comforts his people, so joy is his transforming work rather than mere change of circumstances. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as reversing the silenced joy of judgment (compare 7:34; 16:9), and both see comfort in sorrow as God’s gift.

verses.text: I will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and my people will be satisfied with my goodness,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and my people will be satisfied with my goodness.” Arminian readers see the restoration of worship, with priests provided for through abundant offerings, and the people satisfied by God’s goodness as they live in grateful relationship with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same satisfaction as God’s goodness filling his people, with priest and people alike sustained by his provision. Shared ground: both traditions read “fatness” as abundance from the offerings brought in a restored temple service, and both see satisfaction in the LORD’s goodness as the climax of this oracle.
